newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - PowerGen says results support strategy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - PowerGen says results support strategy.

text.p: Britain's PowerGen Plc turned in annual results in line with expectations on Thursday and announced two southeast Asian projects under its strategy of minimising the effect of increasing competition at home.

The electricity generator said pretax profits before exceptional items for the year were 575 million pounds ($945.9 million), up from 566 million previously, and paid out a dividend of 25.2 pence per share, compared with 21 pence last time.

"The results demonstrate the success of our business strategy in minimising the impact on...profitability of increasing intense competition in the U.K. electricity market," chairman Ed Wallis said in a statement.
Shares in the company were little changed at mid afternoon, off 1-1/2 pence at 692 from an earlier high around 700 pence.
"It is a good set of results and certainly outshines National Power," said Nigel Hawkins, analyst at Yamaichi.
Fellow generator National Power turned in an eight percent fall in year profits to 740 million pounds on Wednesday and raised its dividend nine percent compared with PowerGen's 20 percent rise.

PowerGen said it had agreed to take significant stakes in two independent power projects planned in Indonesia and Thailand, which will cost in total 1.27 billion pounds and increase the company's international capacity by 34 percent.

Existing overseas operations in Germany, Hungary and Australia, along with projects under construction in India, Indonesia and Portugal, should add operating profits of 100 million pounds in five years, group managing director Deryk King told reporters.

The two new projects together with those already underway will give PowerGen interests in a total 7,700 megaWatts of gross generating capacity outside Britain, around half of its domestic interest, with equity investment of 700 million pounds.
PowerGen's share of the British electricity market dipped to 21.6 percent from 23 percent the previous year, partly due to enforced divestment of some plant on competition grounds.
"I am fundamentally rather cautious on the impact of competitive developments in the U.K.," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
But other analysts said the figure compared favourably with National Power's slide in market share to 24 percent from 32 percent, of which over half was due to sell-offs requested by regulators.
"National Power must be a bit concerned about its eroding market share," Hawkins said.
National Power shares, which slipped nearly 20 pence on Wednesday, were down 2.5 pence on Thursday to 543.

PowerGen, which was blocked in its attempts to buy a regional electricity company (Rec) last year by the then Conservative government, will pursue deals with Recs to sell electricity when the British market opens up fully to competition in 1998.
"Right now, we intend to sell our product to the domestic market through the Recs...we believe the Recs will be in a very strong position to defend their electricity business," King said.
Finance director Peter Hickson said the company was looking at a number of potential projects, "any one of (which) could substantially increase the gearing," currently at a modest 34 percent.
He added that if the company did not have any further projects, "then we might obviously look at ways in which we could return additional value".
PowerGen bought back five percent of its shares in December 1996 after spending 400 million pounds on a 10 percent buyback in June, following the government's rejection of its plans to buy a Rec.
National Power, which was also stopped from taking over a Rec last year, hiked its dividend a year ago by 49 percent and made a special dividend payout of one pound per share.
On Thursday, National Power tried to defend itself against a one-off tax on excess profits proposed by the new Labour government, which came to power in a landslide election victory on May 1.
The generator said it did not believe it had made excess profits, and that it was not regulated and faced competition, which should exclude it from any tax aimed at regulated monopolies.

PowerGen made no comment on the proposed windfall tax, although Hickson said the company would be making its comments known to the government. "Until we see how the legislation is framed, there is very little we can say," he said.
British finance minister Gordon Brown is set to give details of the proposed tax in an emergency budget, widely expected to be announced on June 10.
($ = 0.607 British Pounds)
